The Abstract, Methods and Conclusion make unquantified series-level statements (no history of thrombosis, oral contraceptive for more than 1 month to be able to fast, no other possible risk factors, CVT confirmed by magnetic resonance venography, thrombophilia and vasculitis assessments that were rollout, fasting women during Ramadan) without naming individual cases; they are copied to each case only as review_only facts. Statements that explicitly cover all patients (all patients used a short course OCP during Ramadan, nine cases used contraceptive pills to delay menstruation, nine patients with CVT admitted to the neurology ward, headache in 9/9 patients, review_only for Case 9 because the table rows disagree) are recorded for the cases they cover.

Cohort symptom counts and percentages in the Abstract, Discussion and Table 1 footnote (headache 9/9, vomiting 5/9, vertigo 4/9, nausea and seizure 33%, papilledema 33%, blurred vision 22%) agree with the symptoms listed in the Table 1 rows only for some symptoms (nausea and seizure) and disagree for others (for example vertigo, vomiting, papilledema, blurred vision and the headache count). Individual facts follow each patient own row and no count was recalculated or reconciled.

The Introduction says patients were admitted during July-August 2014, while the Abstract and Methods say July-August 2014-2015 (two consecutive years); each admission is recorded only as the stated July-August 2014-2015 window.
Table 1 prints some cells without separators (vomiting papilledema, low blood pressure vertigo, warfarin anticonvulsant); they are read as separate listed items without adding wording.
Figure 1 (brain magnetic resonance venography) is cited only for the series, shows no printed patient label, and is not attributed to any patient; its attribution is unresolved.

The Methods list of the most common clinical signs (headache, papilledema, seizures, sensorimotor deficit, decreased level of consciousness, hemorrhage) is an aggregate statement and is not mapped to individual cases beyond the Table 1 rows; one patient passed away is mapped to Case 9 only through the table cell and footnote that record the single death.

The Case 9 headache comes only from the statements that headache occurred in 9/9 patients; the Case 9 table row does not list it and only eight rows do, so it is kept review_only (count mismatch recorded as an ambiguity).

The Discussion hypothesis about dehydration, comparisons with other published series, regional mortality and incidence figures, and the Introduction general short course pill formulation are not patient facts, and no ingredients or doses are recorded for the cases.

limitations: Table 1 prints Age and Duration of hospital stay as bare numbers without units, so no years or days are recorded; only the follow-up period column states month.

The Abstract, Methods and Conclusion make unquantified series-level statements (no history of thrombosis, oral contraceptive for more than 1 month to be able to fast, no other possible risk factors, CVT confirmed by magnetic resonance venography, thrombophilia and vasculitis assessments that were rollout, fasting women during Ramadan) without naming individual cases; they are copied to each case only as review_only facts. Statements that explicitly cover all patients (all patients used a short course OCP during Ramadan, nine cases used contraceptive pills to delay menstruation, nine patients with CVT admitted to the neurology ward, headache in 9/9 patients, review_only for Case 9 because the table rows disagree) are recorded for the cases they cover.

Cohort symptom counts and percentages in the Abstract, Discussion and Table 1 footnote (headache 9/9, vomiting 5/9, vertigo 4/9, nausea and seizure 33%, papilledema 33%, blurred vision 22%) agree with the symptoms listed in the Table 1 rows only for some symptoms (nausea and seizure) and disagree for others (for example vertigo, vomiting, papilledema, blurred vision and the headache count). Individual facts follow each patient own row and no count was recalculated or reconciled.

The Introduction says patients were admitted during July-August 2014, while the Abstract and Methods say July-August 2014-2015 (two consecutive years); each admission is recorded only as the stated July-August 2014-2015 window.
Table 1 prints some cells without separators (vomiting papilledema, low blood pressure vertigo, warfarin anticonvulsant); they are read as separate listed items without adding wording.
Figure 1 (brain magnetic resonance venography) is cited only for the series, shows no printed patient label, and is not attributed to any patient; its attribution is unresolved.

The Methods list of the most common clinical signs (headache, papilledema, seizures, sensorimotor deficit, decreased level of consciousness, hemorrhage) is an aggregate statement and is not mapped to individual cases beyond the Table 1 rows; one patient passed away is mapped to Case 9 only through the table cell and footnote that record the single death.

The Case 9 headache comes only from the statements that headache occurred in 9/9 patients; the Case 9 table row does not list it and only eight rows do, so it is kept review_only (count mismatch recorded as an ambiguity).

The Discussion hypothesis about dehydration, comparisons with other published series, regional mortality and incidence figures, and the Introduction general short course pill formulation are not patient facts, and no ingredients or doses are recorded for the cases.

limitations: Table 1 prints Age and Duration of hospital stay as bare numbers without units, so no years or days are recorded; only the follow-up period column states month.

The Abstract, Methods and Conclusion make unquantified series-level statements (no history of thrombosis, oral contraceptive for more than 1 month to be able to fast, no other possible risk factors, CVT confirmed by magnetic resonance venography, thrombophilia and vasculitis assessments that were rollout, fasting women during Ramadan) without naming individual cases; they are copied to each case only as review_only facts. Statements that explicitly cover all patients (all patients used a short course OCP during Ramadan, nine cases used contraceptive pills to delay menstruation, nine patients with CVT admitted to the neurology ward, headache in 9/9 patients, review_only for Case 9 because the table rows disagree) are recorded for the cases they cover.

Cohort symptom counts and percentages in the Abstract, Discussion and Table 1 footnote (headache 9/9, vomiting 5/9, vertigo 4/9, nausea and seizure 33%, papilledema 33%, blurred vision 22%) agree with the symptoms listed in the Table 1 rows only for some symptoms (nausea and seizure) and disagree for others (for example vertigo, vomiting, papilledema, blurred vision and the headache count). Individual facts follow each patient own row and no count was recalculated or reconciled.

The Introduction says patients were admitted during July-August 2014, while the Abstract and Methods say July-August 2014-2015 (two consecutive years); each admission is recorded only as the stated July-August 2014-2015 window.
Table 1 prints some cells without separators (vomiting papilledema, low blood pressure vertigo, warfarin anticonvulsant); they are read as separate listed items without adding wording.
Figure 1 (brain magnetic resonance venography) is cited only for the series, shows no printed patient label, and is not attributed to any patient; its attribution is unresolved.

The Methods list of the most common clinical signs (headache, papilledema, seizures, sensorimotor deficit, decreased level of consciousness, hemorrhage) is an aggregate statement and is not mapped to individual cases beyond the Table 1 rows; one patient passed away is mapped to Case 9 only through the table cell and footnote that record the single death.

The Case 9 headache comes only from the statements that headache occurred in 9/9 patients; the Case 9 table row does not list it and only eight rows do, so it is kept review_only (count mismatch recorded as an ambiguity).

The Discussion hypothesis about dehydration, comparisons with other published series, regional mortality and incidence figures, and the Introduction general short course pill formulation are not patient facts, and no ingredients or doses are recorded for the cases.

claims.text: Case 4 is a woman aged 39 of Kurdish ethnicity, admitted to the neurology ward of Tohid Hospital of Sanandaj in July-August 2014-2015 as one of nine patients with cerebral venous thrombosis. The series states that all patients had used a short course oral contraceptive pill during Ramadan to delay women’s menstruation. limitations: Table 1 prints Age and Duration of hospital stay as bare numbers without units, so no years or days are recorded; only the follow-up period column states month.

The Abstract, Methods and Conclusion make unquantified series-level statements (no history of thrombosis, oral contraceptive for more than 1 month to be able to fast, no other possible risk factors, CVT confirmed by magnetic resonance venography, thrombophilia and vasculitis assessments that were rollout, fasting women during Ramadan) without naming individual cases; they are copied to each case only as review_only facts. Statements that explicitly cover all patients (all patients used a short course OCP during Ramadan, nine cases used contraceptive pills to delay menstruation, nine patients with CVT admitted to the neurology ward, headache in 9/9 patients, review_only for Case 9 because the table rows disagree) are recorded for the cases they cover.

Cohort symptom counts and percentages in the Abstract, Discussion and Table 1 footnote (headache 9/9, vomiting 5/9, vertigo 4/9, nausea and seizure 33%, papilledema 33%, blurred vision 22%) agree with the symptoms listed in the Table 1 rows only for some symptoms (nausea and seizure) and disagree for others (for example vertigo, vomiting, papilledema, blurred vision and the headache count). Individual facts follow each patient own row and no count was recalculated or reconciled.

The Introduction says patients were admitted during July-August 2014, while the Abstract and Methods say July-August 2014-2015 (two consecutive years); each admission is recorded only as the stated July-August 2014-2015 window.
Table 1 prints some cells without separators (vomiting papilledema, low blood pressure vertigo, warfarin anticonvulsant); they are read as separate listed items without adding wording.
Figure 1 (brain magnetic resonance venography) is cited only for the series, shows no printed patient label, and is not attributed to any patient; its attribution is unresolved.

The Methods list of the most common clinical signs (headache, papilledema, seizures, sensorimotor deficit, decreased level of consciousness, hemorrhage) is an aggregate statement and is not mapped to individual cases beyond the Table 1 rows; one patient passed away is mapped to Case 9 only through the table cell and footnote that record the single death.

The Case 9 headache comes only from the statements that headache occurred in 9/9 patients; the Case 9 table row does not list it and only eight rows do, so it is kept review_only (count mismatch recorded as an ambiguity).

The Discussion hypothesis about dehydration, comparisons with other published series, regional mortality and incidence figures, and the Introduction general short course pill formulation are not patient facts, and no ingredients or doses are recorded for the cases.

limitations: Table 1 prints Age and Duration of hospital stay as bare numbers without units, so no years or days are recorded; only the follow-up period column states month.

The Abstract, Methods and Conclusion make unquantified series-level statements (no history of thrombosis, oral contraceptive for more than 1 month to be able to fast, no other possible risk factors, CVT confirmed by magnetic resonance venography, thrombophilia and vasculitis assessments that were rollout, fasting women during Ramadan) without naming individual cases; they are copied to each case only as review_only facts. Statements that explicitly cover all patients (all patients used a short course OCP during Ramadan, nine cases used contraceptive pills to delay menstruation, nine patients with CVT admitted to the neurology ward, headache in 9/9 patients, review_only for Case 9 because the table rows disagree) are recorded for the cases they cover.

Cohort symptom counts and percentages in the Abstract, Discussion and Table 1 footnote (headache 9/9, vomiting 5/9, vertigo 4/9, nausea and seizure 33%, papilledema 33%, blurred vision 22%) agree with the symptoms listed in the Table 1 rows only for some symptoms (nausea and seizure) and disagree for others (for example vertigo, vomiting, papilledema, blurred vision and the headache count). Individual facts follow each patient own row and no count was recalculated or reconciled.

The Introduction says patients were admitted during July-August 2014, while the Abstract and Methods say July-August 2014-2015 (two consecutive years); each admission is recorded only as the stated July-August 2014-2015 window.
Table 1 prints some cells without separators (vomiting papilledema, low blood pressure vertigo, warfarin anticonvulsant); they are read as separate listed items without adding wording.
Figure 1 (brain magnetic resonance venography) is cited only for the series, shows no printed patient label, and is not attributed to any patient; its attribution is unresolved.

The Methods list of the most common clinical signs (headache, papilledema, seizures, sensorimotor deficit, decreased level of consciousness, hemorrhage) is an aggregate statement and is not mapped to individual cases beyond the Table 1 rows; one patient passed away is mapped to Case 9 only through the table cell and footnote that record the single death.

The Case 9 headache comes only from the statements that headache occurred in 9/9 patients; the Case 9 table row does not list it and only eight rows do, so it is kept review_only (count mismatch recorded as an ambiguity).

The Discussion hypothesis about dehydration, comparisons with other published series, regional mortality and incidence figures, and the Introduction general short course pill formulation are not patient facts, and no ingredients or doses are recorded for the cases.

limitations: Table 1 prints Age and Duration of hospital stay as bare numbers without units, so no years or days are recorded; only the follow-up period column states month.

The Abstract, Methods and Conclusion make unquantified series-level statements (no history of thrombosis, oral contraceptive for more than 1 month to be able to fast, no other possible risk factors, CVT confirmed by magnetic resonance venography, thrombophilia and vasculitis assessments that were rollout, fasting women during Ramadan) without naming individual cases; they are copied to each case only as review_only facts. Statements that explicitly cover all patients (all patients used a short course OCP during Ramadan, nine cases used contraceptive pills to delay menstruation, nine patients with CVT admitted to the neurology ward, headache in 9/9 patients, review_only for Case 9 because the table rows disagree) are recorded for the cases they cover.

Cohort symptom counts and percentages in the Abstract, Discussion and Table 1 footnote (headache 9/9, vomiting 5/9, vertigo 4/9, nausea and seizure 33%, papilledema 33%, blurred vision 22%) agree with the symptoms listed in the Table 1 rows only for some symptoms (nausea and seizure) and disagree for others (for example vertigo, vomiting, papilledema, blurred vision and the headache count). Individual facts follow each patient own row and no count was recalculated or reconciled.

The Introduction says patients were admitted during July-August 2014, while the Abstract and Methods say July-August 2014-2015 (two consecutive years); each admission is recorded only as the stated July-August 2014-2015 window.
Table 1 prints some cells without separators (vomiting papilledema, low blood pressure vertigo, warfarin anticonvulsant); they are read as separate listed items without adding wording.
Figure 1 (brain magnetic resonance venography) is cited only for the series, shows no printed patient label, and is not attributed to any patient; its attribution is unresolved.

The Methods list of the most common clinical signs (headache, papilledema, seizures, sensorimotor deficit, decreased level of consciousness, hemorrhage) is an aggregate statement and is not mapped to individual cases beyond the Table 1 rows; one patient passed away is mapped to Case 9 only through the table cell and footnote that record the single death.

The Case 9 headache comes only from the statements that headache occurred in 9/9 patients; the Case 9 table row does not list it and only eight rows do, so it is kept review_only (count mismatch recorded as an ambiguity).

The Discussion hypothesis about dehydration, comparisons with other published series, regional mortality and incidence figures, and the Introduction general short course pill formulation are not patient facts, and no ingredients or doses are recorded for the cases.

limitations: Table 1 prints Age and Duration of hospital stay as bare numbers without units, so no years or days are recorded; only the follow-up period column states month.

The Abstract, Methods and Conclusion make unquantified series-level statements (no history of thrombosis, oral contraceptive for more than 1 month to be able to fast, no other possible risk factors, CVT confirmed by magnetic resonance venography, thrombophilia and vasculitis assessments that were rollout, fasting women during Ramadan) without naming individual cases; they are copied to each case only as review_only facts. Statements that explicitly cover all patients (all patients used a short course OCP during Ramadan, nine cases used contraceptive pills to delay menstruation, nine patients with CVT admitted to the neurology ward, headache in 9/9 patients, review_only for Case 9 because the table rows disagree) are recorded for the cases they cover.

Cohort symptom counts and percentages in the Abstract, Discussion and Table 1 footnote (headache 9/9, vomiting 5/9, vertigo 4/9, nausea and seizure 33%, papilledema 33%, blurred vision 22%) agree with the symptoms listed in the Table 1 rows only for some symptoms (nausea and seizure) and disagree for others (for example vertigo, vomiting, papilledema, blurred vision and the headache count). Individual facts follow each patient own row and no count was recalculated or reconciled.

The Introduction says patients were admitted during July-August 2014, while the Abstract and Methods say July-August 2014-2015 (two consecutive years); each admission is recorded only as the stated July-August 2014-2015 window.
Table 1 prints some cells without separators (vomiting papilledema, low blood pressure vertigo, warfarin anticonvulsant); they are read as separate listed items without adding wording.
Figure 1 (brain magnetic resonance venography) is cited only for the series, shows no printed patient label, and is not attributed to any patient; its attribution is unresolved.

The Methods list of the most common clinical signs (headache, papilledema, seizures, sensorimotor deficit, decreased level of consciousness, hemorrhage) is an aggregate statement and is not mapped to individual cases beyond the Table 1 rows; one patient passed away is mapped to Case 9 only through the table cell and footnote that record the single death.

The Case 9 headache comes only from the statements that headache occurred in 9/9 patients; the Case 9 table row does not list it and only eight rows do, so it is kept review_only (count mismatch recorded as an ambiguity).

The Discussion hypothesis about dehydration, comparisons with other published series, regional mortality and incidence figures, and the Introduction general short course pill formulation are not patient facts, and no ingredients or doses are recorded for the cases.

attribution_limitations: The Abstract, Methods and Conclusion describe the series with unquantified plural statements (Patients, They, CVT was diagnosed, the paraclinical assessments were conducted, in fasting woman during Ramadan) that do not name individual cases. They are kept for this case only as review_only facts and are not accepted as individually confirmed.
Table 1 prints Age and Duration of hospital stay as bare numbers without units; only the follow-up period column states month.
The Introduction says the study reports patients admitted during July-August 2014, while the Abstract and Methods say July-August 2014-2015 (two consecutive years).

Cohort-level symptom counts and percentages in the Abstract, Discussion and Table 1 footnote do not fully agree with the symptoms listed in the Table 1 rows (for example vertigo is listed in more than four rows, and headache is not listed in the Case 9 row).

The Clinical manifestation cell prints "low blood pressure vertigo" and "vomiting papilledema" without separating commas, and the Treatment cell prints "warfarin anticonvulsant" without a conjunction. They are read as separate listed items.
The Hospital discharge outcome cell reads Recovered without naming the condition, the degree of recovery or any residual deficit.

limitations: Table 1 prints Age and Duration of hospital stay as bare numbers without units, so no years or days are recorded; only the follow-up period column states month.

The Abstract, Methods and Conclusion make unquantified series-level statements (no history of thrombosis, oral contraceptive for more than 1 month to be able to fast, no other possible risk factors, CVT confirmed by magnetic resonance venography, thrombophilia and vasculitis assessments that were rollout, fasting women during Ramadan) without naming individual cases; they are copied to each case only as review_only facts. Statements that explicitly cover all patients (all patients used a short course OCP during Ramadan, nine cases used contraceptive pills to delay menstruation, nine patients with CVT admitted to the neurology ward, headache in 9/9 patients, review_only for Case 9 because the table rows disagree) are recorded for the cases they cover.

Cohort symptom counts and percentages in the Abstract, Discussion and Table 1 footnote (headache 9/9, vomiting 5/9, vertigo 4/9, nausea and seizure 33%, papilledema 33%, blurred vision 22%) agree with the symptoms listed in the Table 1 rows only for some symptoms (nausea and seizure) and disagree for others (for example vertigo, vomiting, papilledema, blurred vision and the headache count). Individual facts follow each patient own row and no count was recalculated or reconciled.

The Introduction says patients were admitted during July-August 2014, while the Abstract and Methods say July-August 2014-2015 (two consecutive years); each admission is recorded only as the stated July-August 2014-2015 window.
Table 1 prints some cells without separators (vomiting papilledema, low blood pressure vertigo, warfarin anticonvulsant); they are read as separate listed items without adding wording.
Figure 1 (brain magnetic resonance venography) is cited only for the series, shows no printed patient label, and is not attributed to any patient; its attribution is unresolved.

The Methods list of the most common clinical signs (headache, papilledema, seizures, sensorimotor deficit, decreased level of consciousness, hemorrhage) is an aggregate statement and is not mapped to individual cases beyond the Table 1 rows; one patient passed away is mapped to Case 9 only through the table cell and footnote that record the single death.

The Case 9 headache comes only from the statements that headache occurred in 9/9 patients; the Case 9 table row does not list it and only eight rows do, so it is kept review_only (count mismatch recorded as an ambiguity).

The Discussion hypothesis about dehydration, comparisons with other published series, regional mortality and incidence figures, and the Introduction general short course pill formulation are not patient facts, and no ingredients or doses are recorded for the cases.

attribution_limitations: The Abstract, Methods and Conclusion describe the series with unquantified plural statements (Patients, They, CVT was diagnosed, the paraclinical assessments were conducted, in fasting woman during Ramadan) that do not name individual cases. They are kept for this case only as review_only facts and are not accepted as individually confirmed.
Table 1 prints Age and Duration of hospital stay as bare numbers without units; only the follow-up period column states month.
The Introduction says the study reports patients admitted during July-August 2014, while the Abstract and Methods say July-August 2014-2015 (two consecutive years).

Cohort-level symptom counts and percentages in the Abstract, Discussion and Table 1 footnote do not fully agree with the symptoms listed in the Table 1 rows (for example vertigo is listed in more than four rows, and headache is not listed in the Case 9 row).

Headache is stated for 9/9 patients (100%) in the Abstract and Discussion, but the Case 9 table row lists no headache (it lists low level of consciousness, GCS = 3, tachypnea and double Babinski extensor) and only eight table rows list headache. The Case 9 headache rests only on this aggregate count and is kept review_only.

The Abstract says the patients did not have other possible risk factors for CVT, while Table 1 lists obesity (BMI = 35) in the Pre-disposing factor column for Case 9. The Pre-disposing factor footnote also says predisposing factors were evaluated and excluded, but the Case 9 cell does not read Absent.

The single death is described three ways: due to hemorrhagic infarction (Table 1 cell), massive hemorrhagic infarctions and thrombosis (footnote ***), and large bilateral hemorrhagic venous infarction as the main reason of death (Discussion). The descriptions are compatible but differ in detail, and the Discussion sentence is unlabelled.
The follow-up period cell for Case 9 is a dash.

items.action_text: Admission to the neurology ward of Tohid Hospital of Sanandaj

claims.text: Case 9 is a woman aged 49 of Kurdish ethnicity, admitted to the neurology ward of Tohid Hospital of Sanandaj in July-August 2014-2015 as one of nine patients with cerebral venous thrombosis. The series states that all patients had used a short course oral contraceptive pill during Ramadan to delay women’s menstruation. Table 1 lists low level of consciousness, Glasgow Coma Scale score 3, tachypnea and double Babinski extensor as clinical manifestations.

limitations: Table 1 prints Age and Duration of hospital stay as bare numbers without units, so no years or days are recorded; only the follow-up period column states month.

The Abstract, Methods and Conclusion make unquantified series-level statements (no history of thrombosis, oral contraceptive for more than 1 month to be able to fast, no other possible risk factors, CVT confirmed by magnetic resonance venography, thrombophilia and vasculitis assessments that were rollout, fasting women during Ramadan) without naming individual cases; they are copied to each case only as review_only facts. Statements that explicitly cover all patients (all patients used a short course OCP during Ramadan, nine cases used contraceptive pills to delay menstruation, nine patients with CVT admitted to the neurology ward, headache in 9/9 patients, review_only for Case 9 because the table rows disagree) are recorded for the cases they cover.

Cohort symptom counts and percentages in the Abstract, Discussion and Table 1 footnote (headache 9/9, vomiting 5/9, vertigo 4/9, nausea and seizure 33%, papilledema 33%, blurred vision 22%) agree with the symptoms listed in the Table 1 rows only for some symptoms (nausea and seizure) and disagree for others (for example vertigo, vomiting, papilledema, blurred vision and the headache count). Individual facts follow each patient own row and no count was recalculated or reconciled.

The Introduction says patients were admitted during July-August 2014, while the Abstract and Methods say July-August 2014-2015 (two consecutive years); each admission is recorded only as the stated July-August 2014-2015 window.
Table 1 prints some cells without separators (vomiting papilledema, low blood pressure vertigo, warfarin anticonvulsant); they are read as separate listed items without adding wording.
Figure 1 (brain magnetic resonance venography) is cited only for the series, shows no printed patient label, and is not attributed to any patient; its attribution is unresolved.

The Methods list of the most common clinical signs (headache, papilledema, seizures, sensorimotor deficit, decreased level of consciousness, hemorrhage) is an aggregate statement and is not mapped to individual cases beyond the Table 1 rows; one patient passed away is mapped to Case 9 only through the table cell and footnote that record the single death.

The Case 9 headache comes only from the statements that headache occurred in 9/9 patients; the Case 9 table row does not list it and only eight rows do, so it is kept review_only (count mismatch recorded as an ambiguity).

The Discussion hypothesis about dehydration, comparisons with other published series, regional mortality and incidence figures, and the Introduction general short course pill formulation are not patient facts, and no ingredients or doses are recorded for the cases.
